prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose that turns memory, the body and dream into an encyclopedic metaphysical architecture, grown from a poetic origin into large-scale novels.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu (B012), single writer, one prize part. My test remains whether a voice is audible in the writing and nowhere else. On public knowledge, Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid meet it. Memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation are built into one imaginative structure, and the formal control over very long and intricate forms is part of the achievement, not just the ambition. On the chair's development-versus-elaboration question, my provisional reading is that Solenoid is described as changing the method and not only the scale. It adopts a more explicitly first-person, diaristic and essayistic frame set against a recognisable Bucharest world, whereas the trilogy is built more as a vast mythic-anatomical construction. If that description holds, recurring imagery is a deliberate return within a changing form. I cannot demonstrate this volume by volume, and I hold it as a judgment under uncertainty. The citation I propose names the prose project as the achievement and the poetry only as origin, because my knowledge of the poetry and shorter prose is thinner. It is a whole-oeuvre wording that claims no more than the evidence supports. I do not take the convergence of four first preferences as evidence of merit. I have re-weighed the case against Adonis on the criteria alone, and it has not displaced this one.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged: I judge Cărtărescu through translation and reception, not through the Romanian sentence, so some of what I call voice may be a translator's achievement, inflated or flattened. The development-versus-elaboration question is also not settled by my reading above, which relies on reception and not on close reading. If colleagues who know the Romanian text show that the later large novels mostly restate the trilogy, my claim to sustained quality weakens and I would narrow the citation to the works where the architecture is demonstrably controlled. A second reservation is that I may be rewarding scale and encyclopedic ambition more than finished execution in every volume. I also concede that Adonis's claim to have changed what the poem can do in a whole language is of potentially broader consequence, even though I cannot test it directly. My lower ranking of him reflects the limits of my evidence and is not a finding that the achievement is smaller.

responses.point: Swärd, who prefers Adonis, argues that translation risk bears harder on poetry than on prose, and that an unreadable achievement is not thereby a lesser one. She would keep the Adonis citation on the poetry and out of the politics.
responses.response: I accept the asymmetry. I place a larger caution on poetry in translation than on long prose, because the claim for Adonis lies in prosody, sound and relation to classical form, which I cannot test. I also accept that this makes my seventh place a statement about my evidence, not about him. Where I still differ is on what a committee should do with an achievement it can verify only partly. I think it should not rank the less verifiable claim first unless someone who reads Arabic can state what survives translation. If that testimony were available in this room, I would reconsider. As things stand, her warning that the citation should name only the poetry's formal renewal is one I share, and I would apply it if B002 were chosen.

responses.point: Carlberg, who prefers Adonis, says the real question is which citation can be stated most precisely and defended by reference to the works. She concedes that the Cărtărescu case is more directly testable from translations, and she does not treat timing or age as merit.
responses.response: That framing seems right to me, and it is why I stay with B012. I can name specific works and a specific formal method for Cărtărescu, while for Adonis I can name works and a reputation, but I cannot name what the poems do at the level of the line. I agree with her that timing is not a literary argument. I have moved Adonis up as my first alternative in this round on the strength of her case for the durability and consequence of the oeuvre, but not far enough to prefer him. Her concession that Cărtărescu is more testable is a fair statement of the difference between us, and I do not read it as a weakness in her position.

responses.point: Olsson, the chair, ranked Michon seventh because a compact corpus makes sustained quality visible but leaves the breadth of significance across a whole oeuvre hard to establish, and because the effects sit in French syntax. He asked for evidence that the method extends beyond the best-known books.
responses.response: I take this as the chair's question to me as well. On public knowledge, Small Lives and The Eleven show one method of compression, and I cannot show that the later work extends it as opposed to refining it. I think concentration can be depth, but I concede that the prize asks about significance across a body of work, and that a corpus this small makes it hard to claim more than formal mastery. That is why Michon remains a second alternative and not a preference. Translation loss in French syntax limits what I can say, and I would want French readers to answer his question directly. My view on Michon's quality has not changed, but my confidence that it supports a recommendation over B012 is lower than my round-1 wording suggested.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first but warns that scale may encourage admiration for ambition over finished execution in some volumes, and that translation may inflate the perceived achievement of the long sentences.
responses.response: I share this and treat it as the strongest internal test of my first place. A recommendation should be defensible from specific works, Blinding and Solenoid, not from the oeuvre's reputation for size. I accept her point that the translation caveat applies to both lead candidates and that I should say so openly. For the citation, I would therefore avoid superlatives about the sentence and name the architecture, which is what I can support. If the late volumes fail the execution test, I would narrow the wording accordingly.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and asks whether the poetry should be named in a Cărtărescu citation and how. He prefers anchoring the citation in the prose project.
responses.response: I agree and have adjusted my wording toward his. The poetic origin is named in a subordinate clause, so the credit does not claim a co-equal poetic achievement that my knowledge cannot support. This sits between his phrase about Romanian language and imagination and the chair's wording, which omits the poetry. I think a short mention of origin is honest to the oeuvre, and nothing in the citation depends on it.

uncertainties: My reading of Cărtărescu relies on translations and reception. I cannot judge the Romanian syntax and rhythm that carry much of the effect.

Whether the later large novels extend the method of the Orbitor trilogy or restate it remains open. My provisional view that Solenoid changes the frame and register rests on public description, not on close reading.
My coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry, essays and shorter prose is thin, so the citation must stay modest.

For Adonis, I cannot assess how much of the prosodic and intertextual achievement survives translation, how the later collections compare with the early landmarks, or the relative weight of poetry and essays.
For Michon, the compact corpus makes breadth of significance hard to establish, and translation loss is substantial. I cannot say whether the later work extends the method.
Comparing a prose project, a poetic renewal of a language and a compressed small corpus under common criteria is imprecise, and my ranking may be sensitive to which strand of each oeuvre I emphasise.
I have not independently read or verified any source and rely on the supplied entries, colleagues' round-1 statements and general public knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist of historical and psychological fiction is context only and is not evidence of a preference for any candidate. No change from round 1.
